# Part I: The Palmer Penguins Dataset

## Dataset Overview

The Palmer Penguins dataset (Gorman et al., 2014):

- Collected at Palmer Station, Antarctica (2007-2009)
- Three species: Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo
- Morphometric measurements: bill length, bill depth, flipper length, body mass
- 344 observations (333 complete cases)

**Our goal:** Predict body mass from morphometric measurements

## Why Palmer Penguins?

Advantages over the iris dataset (Horst et al., 2022):

- **Realistic data:** Missing values, unbalanced groups
- **Intuitive variables:** Flipper length vs. sepal width
- **Documented provenance:** Published research data
- **Ethical considerations:** No association with eugenics research

## Loading the Data

```{r}
library(palmerpenguins)
data(penguins)

glimpse(penguins)
```

## Handling Missing Values

```{r}
penguins |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "missing")
```

For this analysis, we remove incomplete cases:

```{r}
penguins_clean <- penguins |> drop_na()
cat("Complete cases:", nrow(penguins_clean))
```


# Part II: Exploratory Data Analysis

## Species Distribution

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(penguins_clean, aes(x = species, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = species_colors) +
  labs(title = "Sample Sizes by Species", y = "Count") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Body Mass by Species

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(penguins_clean, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = species, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = species_colors) +
  labs(x = "Body Mass (g)", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Correlation Matrix

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
numeric_vars <- penguins_clean |>
  select(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)
correlation_matrix <- cor(numeric_vars)
corrplot(correlation_matrix, method = "color", type = "upper",
         addCoef.col = "black", number.cex = 0.8)
```

## Key Correlations

| Predictor | Correlation with Body Mass |
|-----------|---------------------------|
| Flipper length | **0.87** |
| Bill length | 0.60 |
| Bill depth | 0.43 |

**Flipper length** shows the strongest relationship with body mass.


# Part III: Simple Linear Regression

## Model Specification

Simple linear regression model:

$$\text{body\_mass}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{flipper\_length}_i + \epsilon_i$$

where $\epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$

```{r}
model_simple <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = penguins_clean)
```

## Model Results

```{r}
summary(model_simple)
```

## Interpreting Coefficients

```{r}
coef(model_simple)
```

- **Intercept**: -5781 g (extrapolation beyond data range)
- **Slope**: 49.7 g per mm of flipper length

**Interpretation**: Each additional millimeter of flipper length is associated
with approximately 50 grams of body mass.

## Visualization

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(penguins_clean, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "black", se = TRUE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = species_colors) +
  labs(x = "Flipper Length (mm)", y = "Body Mass (g)")
```

## Model Performance

```{r}
simple_metrics <- glance(model_simple)
cat("R-squared:", round(simple_metrics$r.squared, 3), "\n")
cat("RMSE:", round(sqrt(mean(model_simple$residuals^2)), 1), "g\n")
```

The simple model explains **76%** of variance in body mass.


# Part IV: Multiple Regression

## Adding More Predictors

```{r}
model_multiple <- lm(body_mass_g ~ bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm +
                       flipper_length_mm, data = penguins_clean)
summary(model_multiple)
```

## Multicollinearity Check

Variance Inflation Factors (VIF):

```{r}
vif_values <- vif(model_multiple)
print(round(vif_values, 2))
```

**Rule of thumb**: VIF > 5 indicates concerning multicollinearity

## Concerning Result

Notice the coefficient for **bill depth**:

```{r}
coef(model_multiple)["bill_depth_mm"]
```

**Bill depth has a negative coefficient!**

But wait - we saw a positive correlation earlier...


# Part V: Simpson's Paradox

## The Paradox Revealed

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
p1 <- ggplot(penguins_clean, aes(x = bill_depth_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Overall: Negative", x = "Bill Depth (mm)", y = "Body Mass (g)")

p2 <- ggplot(penguins_clean, aes(x = bill_depth_mm, y = body_mass_g,
                                  color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = species_colors) +
  labs(title = "Within Species: Positive", x = "Bill Depth (mm)",
       y = "Body Mass (g)")
p1 + p2
```

## What's Happening?

**Simpson's Paradox** (Pearl, 2014):

- Overall correlation: **negative**
- Within-species correlation: **positive**

**Why?**

- Gentoo penguins: large bodies, **shallow** bills
- Adelie penguins: smaller bodies, **deeper** bills

Species acts as a **confounding variable**.

## The Solution

Include species in the model to properly account for this confounding:

```{r}
model_species <- lm(body_mass_g ~ bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm +
                      flipper_length_mm + species, data = penguins_clean)
```


# Part VI: Species-Aware Models

## Model Results

```{r}
summary(model_species)
```

## Coefficient Comparison

```{r}
tibble(
  Term = c("Bill Depth"),
  Without_Species = coef(model_multiple)["bill_depth_mm"],
  With_Species = coef(model_species)["bill_depth_mm"]
) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 1)))
```

After controlling for species, bill depth shows the **expected positive**
relationship with body mass.

## Coefficient Plot

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
coef_df <- tidy(model_species, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(term = fct_reorder(term, estimate))

ggplot(coef_df, aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), height = 0.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#2E8B57") +
  labs(x = "Coefficient Estimate (g)", y = NULL)
```

## Model Performance Improvement

```{r}
tibble(
  Model = c("Simple", "Multiple", "Species-Aware"),
  R_squared = c(
    summary(model_simple)$r.squared,
    summary(model_multiple)$r.squared,
    summary(model_species)$r.squared
  ),
  RMSE = c(
    sqrt(mean(model_simple$residuals^2)),
    sqrt(mean(model_multiple$residuals^2)),
    sqrt(mean(model_species$residuals^2))
  )
) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 3)))
```


# Part VII: Model Diagnostics

## Diagnostic Plots

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model_species)
```

## Interpretation

- **Residuals vs Fitted**: No clear pattern (linearity OK)
- **Q-Q Plot**: Approximately normal residuals
- **Scale-Location**: Relatively constant spread
- **Residuals vs Leverage**: No high-leverage outliers

## Prediction Accuracy

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
predictions <- predict(model_species)
results_df <- penguins_clean |>
  mutate(predicted = predictions, residual = body_mass_g - predicted)

ggplot(results_df, aes(x = predicted, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = species_colors) +
  labs(x = "Predicted Body Mass (g)", y = "Actual Body Mass (g)") +
  coord_equal()
```


# Part VIII: Cross-Validation

## Why Cross-Validation?

- Training R-squared can be **overly optimistic**
- Cross-validation provides honest performance estimates
- Essential for comparing models

## 10-Fold CV Setup

```{r}
library(caret)
set.seed(42)
train_control <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)
```

## Cross-Validation Results

```{r}
cv_simple <- train(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm,
                   data = penguins_clean, method = "lm",
                   trControl = train_control)

cv_species <- train(body_mass_g ~ bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm +
                      flipper_length_mm + species,
                    data = penguins_clean, method = "lm",
                    trControl = train_control)
```

## CV Performance Comparison

```{r}
tibble(
  Model = c("Simple", "Species-Aware"),
  CV_RMSE = c(cv_simple$results$RMSE, cv_species$results$RMSE),
  CV_R_squared = c(cv_simple$results$Rsquared, cv_species$results$Rsquared)
) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 3)))
```


# Part IX: Key Takeaways

## Summary

1. **Flipper length** is the strongest single predictor of body mass
2. **Simpson's Paradox**: Always check for confounding variables
3. **Species-aware models** resolve the paradox and improve fit
4. **Model diagnostics** confirm assumptions are reasonable
5. **Cross-validation** provides honest performance estimates

## Best Practices

- Explore data visually before modeling
- Check for confounding variables
- Include relevant covariates
- Validate with held-out data
- Report honest performance metrics

## Model Performance Summary

| Model | R-squared | CV RMSE (g) |
|-------|-----------|-------------|
| Simple (flipper only) | 0.759 | ~390 |
| Multiple (no species) | 0.779 | ~380 |
| Species-aware | 0.868 | ~290 |

The species-aware model reduces prediction error by **~25%**.
